dedupe_keys.name: realistic worst case for geostationary satellites from a fast solar wind stream horne glauert meredith and others 2018

description: This case study builds a realistic worst case for satellites in geostationary orbit from a fast solar wind stream lasting five days or more, the kind of event that drives internal charging and electrostatic discharge. Richard Horne of the British Antarctic Survey with co-authors from the Surrey Space Centre and Boston University used a physical radiation belt model to compute the maximum electron flux above 2 MeV, finding that flux tends toward a ceiling after five days and stays high for five more, comparable to a 1-in-150-year event from an independent statistical analysis. About 2.4 to 2.5 mm of aluminium shielding would be needed to keep internal charging currents below NASA guidelines, much more than is used today. Coverage is the geostationary belt used for telecommunications, broadcasting and navigation augmentation. Format and access: an open access Space Weather article (2018) on PubMed Central. Licence: CC-BY-4.0; free. Caveats: results come from one model and a constructed scenario, and satellite designs vary widely in shielding. The authors conclude that geostationary satellites are more at risk from such a stream than from a Carrington-type storm, which informs hazard exposure and resilience studies of space infrastructure. Related catalogue records are the satellite cable internal charging worst-case dataset and the UK space weather reasonable worst-case scenarios.

name: Realistic worst case for geostationary satellites from a fast solar wind stream (Horne, Glauert, Meredith and others, 2018)
outcomes: Electron flux above 2 MeV at geostationary orbit approaches a 1-in-150-year level after 5 days; about 2.4 to 2.5 mm of aluminium shielding would be needed to keep internal charging below NASA guidelines, far more than typical, so many satellites would report discharge anomalies and some could be lost.
